title: Quantum-Classical Crossover in Fault-Tolerant Quantum Dynamics Simulation
hook: A new paper puts an actual number on 'when do quantum computers win': about 2 hours and 370,000 qubits to beat 100 years of classical computing on one benchmark physics problem.
key_points: Researchers pin down a concrete 'crossover': when a fault-tolerant quantum computer beats the best classical algorithms.
For a 100-site 1D benchmark, quantum simulation needs ~2 hours and ~370,000 physical qubits.
The best classical method (tensor networks) would need roughly 100 years for the same task.
For 2D systems, where classical methods choke on entanglement, quantum could finish in minutes.
A 10x lower hardware error rate cuts the needed qubits and runtime by at least another 10x.
content_html: According to a new arXiv preprint led by Jinzhao Sun and collaborators, quantum computers may not need to be enormous to beat classical supercomputers at real physics problems — just precisely engineered. The team pins down a concrete "crossover point": the exact hardware needed for an error-corrected quantum computer to outperform the best classical algorithms at simulating how a many-body quantum system evolves over time.
extra_html: For a standard 100-site test system, the researchers calculate that a fault-tolerant quantum computer would need about 370,000 physical qubits and roughly 2 hours — while the best classical approach, tensor networks, would take about 100 years. In two-dimensional systems, where entanglement grows too fast for classical methods to track at all, they project quantum runtimes of just minutes. Improving hardware error rates by a factor of 10 shrinks both the qubit count and runtime by at least another order of magnitude, giving engineers concrete numbers to build toward.

related.title: Quantum Proofs Really Are More Powerful Than Classical Ones
related.hook: For 20+ years it was open whether a 'quantum-shaped' proof gives a quantum computer more power than checking an ordinary one. Researchers just found strong evidence that it does.

related.title: Qubits and Quantum Computing
related.hook: A normal bit is a 0 or a 1. A qubit can be both at once — and linking many of them lets a quantum computer explore a staggering number of possibilities together.
